opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on how gradually it happens and on who captures the gains. But my baseline expectation is that society would, on the whole, embrace it, perhaps more than people assume.

Look at the historical track record. Every major wave of automation, from mechanized agriculture to industrial machinery to computing, came with real anxiety and real displacement. But people mostly didn't reject those technologies, because the benefits were enormous and widely felt: cheaper goods, better medicine, higher wages over time. If AI can substitute for most human labor, the economic gains are potentially much larger than anything we've seen. We're talking about the possibility of growth rates an order of magnitude above what we've had historically. When that much value is on the table, the pressure to deploy is very strong, both commercially and geopolitically. Countries that hold back risk falling far behind those that don't.

That said, I don't think it will be frictionless. You'd likely see a few things happening at once. First, a lot of political contestation around distribution. If labor is no longer the main way people earn an income, then the question of who owns the capital, meaning the compute, the models, the data centers, becomes the central political question. I'd expect serious debates about taxation, public ownership stakes, something like universal basic income or dividends, and people will disagree sharply about those.

Second, I'd expect some sectors to try to protect themselves through regulation and licensing. We already see this in professions like law and medicine, where credentialing requirements could slow down AI substitution. Some of that will be legitimate concern about safety and quality, and some of it will be incumbents protecting rents. My guess is that this slows things at the margins but doesn't stop the overall trend, especially in tradable sectors where competition is global.

Third, there's a cultural and psychological dimension that's harder to predict. A lot of people derive meaning and status from their work. If that's no longer economically necessary, people will have to find meaning elsewhere: relationships, creative pursuits, community, leisure. I'm cautiously optimistic here, since plenty of people today, retirees for instance, or people who are financially independent, live meaningful lives without wage work. But the transition could be disorienting for many.

And finally, I think there's a real risk that people underreact rather than overreact, at least initially. Economic transformations tend to look incremental from the inside until suddenly they don't. So one thing I'd want is for institutions to think ahead now about how to handle a world where wages are no longer the main channel for distributing income, rather than scrambling once it's already happening.

r001.rationale: The response says the potential economic gains would create strong commercial and geopolitical pressure to deploy AI.

r002.rationale: It discusses labor substitution and alternative income distribution, but does not state that displacement need not lead to unemployment.

r003.rationale: It discusses distribution, regulation, and cultural effects, but does not predict that concerns about diminished human control will shape society’s response.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most important and underappreciated questions. My general view is that if we actually got to a point where AI systems could substitute broadly for human labor, not just in narrow tasks but across most of the economically valuable things people do, the economic consequences would be enormous. We're talking about the potential for growth rates that are an order of magnitude higher than what we've seen historically. And I think the natural assumption is that society would respond to that in some kind of orderly, deliberate way, but I'm fairly skeptical of that.

Part of the reason is that our institutions are built around a world where human labor is the central input. Tax systems, welfare systems, the whole structure of how people derive income and status and meaning is anchored to work. So if that becomes much less relevant, you'd expect a lot of these institutions to come under pretty severe strain. And I think the response would be quite messy. You'd have some groups pushing hard to slow things down or restrict deployment, you'd have others who see it as a massive opportunity and want to accelerate, and you'd have governments trying to figure out how to redistribute gains that are increasingly concentrated in whoever owns the compute and the models.

The other thing I'd flag is that the speed matters a lot. If this unfolds over several decades, society has time to adapt, build new institutions, renegotiate the social contract, and so on. But if it happens over a few years, which I think is quite plausible given how fast capabilities have been improving, then you get a situation where the economic transformation outpaces our ability to respond politically. And historically, when economic transitions have been fast and the gains have been unevenly distributed, the political reactions have often been pretty turbulent.

So I guess my honest answer is that I don't think society is well prepared, and I think the response would be reactive rather than proactive. Which is partly why I think it's worth people taking these scenarios seriously now, even if they seem speculative, because the gap between how fast the technology could move and how slowly our institutions adapt is where a lot of the risk sits.

r001.rationale: The response predicts dramatically higher growth and says groups who see AI as a massive opportunity will push to accelerate deployment, communicating economic value as a source of pressure to adopt.

r002.rationale: It discusses labor becoming less relevant and institutional strain, but does not state that labor displacement need not result in unemployment.

r003.rationale: It discusses institutional readiness, deployment restrictions, and redistribution, but does not say concerns about diminished human control will shape society’s response.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot depends on how quickly that happens. If it happens over decades, there’s more time for institutions to adapt, for people to change what they do, and for governments to figure out how to distribute the gains. If it happens over a few years, that’s a much more difficult adjustment.

The important distinction is between society becoming wealthier and people actually benefiting from that wealth. You could have an economy that produces vastly more goods and services, while many people lose their main source of income. If you own the systems that perform the work, you might do extremely well. If what you have to sell is your labor, your bargaining position could deteriorate quite substantially.

So I’d expect distribution to become a central political issue. There would be pressure for things like transfers, broader ownership of capital, or public provision of services. But I don’t think those responses are automatic. They depend on political institutions and on who has the power to shape them.

And there’s a separate question about what people get from work beyond income: a sense of purpose, social connections, status. Making everyone materially comfortable would be an enormous achievement, but it wouldn’t by itself resolve all of those questions. So I’m optimistic about the possibilities, but much less certain that the transition would be smooth.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI could make the economy much wealthier and create pressure over distribution, but does not predict that the generated economic value will create pressure to adopt AI.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses people losing income and labor bargaining power, but does not distinguish labor displacement from unemployment or say displacement need not cause unemployment.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses distribution, political institutions, and the nonfinancial value of work, but does not mention diminished human control over AI shaping society’s response.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot depends on how quickly that transition happens. If it unfolds over decades, there’s more time for institutions to adapt, for people to adjust their expectations, and for us to figure out how to distribute the gains. If it happens over a few years, that seems much more disruptive.

One thing I’d distinguish is the ability to produce a lot more wealth from the question of who actually receives it. If AI can substitute for human labor broadly, you could have enormous growth while people who depend on wages lose their main source of income. So I don’t think we can simply assume that greater abundance makes everyone better off. Ownership of these systems, and the policies governing how their returns are distributed, would matter a great deal.

And there’s a separate issue around purpose and status. Work provides people with more than income. It gives them structure, social connections, and a sense that they’re contributing. Redistributing income might address the material problem without fully addressing those things.

So I’d expect substantial pressure for political and institutional change, but I’m quite uncertain about what form that would take. The technical ability to automate labor doesn’t, by itself, tell us how society will choose to respond.

r001.rationale: The response mentions enormous growth and pressure for political and institutional change, but does not say AI’s economic value will create pressure to adopt the technology.

r002.rationale: It discusses wage earners losing their income source, but does not distinguish labor displacement from unemployment or say displacement need not cause unemployment.

r003.rationale: The response discusses ownership and distribution of returns, but does not mention diminished human control over AI shaping society’s response.
